reply.transliteration: hala w ghala, l-7ajz b-ism mino?
reply.english: Welcome, whose name is the reservation under?

phrases.arabic: الساعَة كَم لازِم أَطلِع مِن الغُرِفَة؟
phrases.transliteration: s-saa3a kam laazim aTla3 min l-ghurfa?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Hello, I have a reservation under the name Nour.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.transliteration: hala w ghala, la7Za min faDlak
dialogue.english: Welcome, one moment please.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.arabic: إي لقيت الحجز، غرفة لشخصين، صح؟
dialogue.transliteration: ee lageet l-7ajz, ghurfa la-shakhSayn, Sa7?
dialogue.english: Yes, I found the reservation, a room for two, right?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Yes, that's right.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.english: How many nights will you stay?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Three nights, God willing.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.arabic: زين، هذا المفتاح، غرفتكم في الدور الثاني
dialogue.transliteration: zeen, hadha l-muftaa7, ghurfatkum fi d-door ith-thaani
dialogue.english: Good, here is the key, your room is on the second floor.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.arabic: إي طبعاً، من السبعة لين العشرة في المطعم
dialogue.transliteration: ee Tab3an, min s-sab3a leen l-3ashra fi l-maT3am
dialogue.english: Yes of course, from seven to ten in the restaurant.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Where's the elevator please?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.english: On the right, after the reception.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Thank you, may God give you strength.

response.arabic: إي عندنا، غرفة لشخصين في الدور الثالث
response.transliteration: ee 3indna, ghurfa la-shakhSayn fi d-door ith-thaalith
response.english: Yes we have, a room for two on the third floor.

pair.english: How much is the price per night?
Is breakfast included with the room?

pair.arabic: الساعَة كَم لازِم أَطلِع مِن الغُرِفَة؟
pair.transliteration: s-saa3a kam laazim aTla3 min l-ghurfa?
pair.english: What time do I need to check out?

lessons.culture: Hotel staff in the Gulf come from many countries, so many will answer in English, but a greeting like "هلا" or "حياك الله" in Arabic is always warmly received. Breakfast is often a buffet, and many locals call the morning meal "ريوق".

exercises.prompt: The receptionist says: "هلا وغلا، تفضل." Say hello and that you have a reservation.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "عندي حجز".

exercises.tip: "عندي" means "I have" and is the everyday way to say it.

exercises.prompt: The receptionist asks: "كم ليلة بتقعدون؟" Say three nights.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "ثلاث ليالي".

exercises.tip: "بتقعدون" means "will you stay", said to more than one person.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أبي غرفة _____." Meaning: I want a room for two people.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أبي" for "I want".

exercises.tip: "أبي" is the everyday Gulf "I want".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ أشوف الغرفة أول؟" Meaning: Can I see the room first?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أقدر أشوف".

exercises.tip: The Gulf "ق" is said like a hard "g": agdar.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where's the elevator?"

too_formal.feedback: "أين" is formal. Everyday Gulf speech says "وين", and most people say "الليفت" for the lift.

exercises.tip: "المصعد" is also understood, but "الليفت" is what you hear.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Thanks, the room is very nice."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "حلوة مرة".

exercises.tip: "مرة" means "very" in Gulf speech.

exercises.prompt: Which one means "How much is the price per night?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "بكم الليلة؟".

exercises.tip: "بكم" means "for how much" and is the everyday price question.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "breakfast" in everyday Gulf speech, besides "الفطور"?

too_formal.feedback: "وجبة الإفطار" is formal, and in Ramadan "إفطار" means the meal that ends the fast.

exercises.tip: "ريوق" is the morning meal in the Gulf. "الفطور" also works at a hotel.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "لشخصين / أبي / غرفة"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أبي غرفة لشخصين".

exercises.tip: The order is want, then room, then for whom.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "الليفت / وين / لو سمحت"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "وين الليفت لو سمحت؟".

exercises.tip: "لو سمحت" goes at the end and keeps the question polite.

phrases.english: Do you have tickets to Dubai?

phrases.arabic: فيه كُرسي فاضي في اَلباص اَلجايِ؟
phrases.transliteration: fiih kursi faadi fi l-baaS l-jaay?

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.arabic: السلام عليكم، أبي أحجز تذكرة باص لدبي
dialogue.transliteration: as-salaamu 3alaykum, abi a7jiz tadhkarat baaS li-dubay
dialogue.english: Peace be upon you, I want to book a bus ticket to Dubai.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.arabic: وعليكم السلام، رايح بس لو رايح جاي؟
dialogue.transliteration: w 3alaykum s-salaam, raayi7 bas low raayi7 jaay?
dialogue.english: And peace upon you, one way only or round trip?

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.english: Round trip, how much is the ticket?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.arabic: خمسة وعشرين درهم، والباص يطلع الساعة تسعة
dialogue.transliteration: khamsa w 3ishreen dirham, w l-baaS yiTla3 s-saa3a tis3a
dialogue.english: Twenty-five dirhams, and the bus leaves at nine.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.english: Yes, if you have your university card.

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.arabic: معاي، هذي بطاقتي. أقدر أدفع بالكرت؟
dialogue.transliteration: ma3ay, hadhi biTaaqati. agdar adfa3 bil-kart?
dialogue.english: I have it, here's my card. Can I pay by card?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.english: About two hours, depending on the traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.english: Good, where exactly is the ticket window?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.arabic: هذا هو قدامك، تفضل هذي تذكرتك
dialogue.transliteration: hadha huwa gidaamak, tfaDDal hadhi tadhkartak
dialogue.english: This is it in front of you, here's your ticket.

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.english: Thank you, may God give you strength.

pair.english: I want to book a bus ticket.
How much is a round-trip ticket?

pair.arabic: فيه كُرسي فاضي في اَلباص اَلجايِ؟
pair.transliteration: fiih kursi faadi fi l-baaS l-jaay?
pair.english: Is there a free seat on the next bus?

response.english: Yes, but only a few seats.

pair.english: What time does the bus leave?
Is there a discount for students?

response.english: Yes, but you need your university card.

lessons.culture: Most people in the UAE and Kuwait travel by car, so intercity buses are mainly used by students and workers. In the UAE a rechargeable Nol card pays for city buses and the metro, and longer trips are booked at the station or by an app.

exercises.prompt: The clerk asks: "رايح بس لو رايح جاي؟" Say round trip.

too_formal.feedback: "ذهاب وإياب" is formal and written. At the counter you say "رايح جاي".

exercises.tip: "رايح" is going, "جاي" is coming, and together they mean round trip.

exercises.prompt: You want to pay. Ask if you can pay by card.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أقدر أدفع بالكرت؟".

exercises.tip: "كرت" is the everyday word for a bank card.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أبي أحجز _____ باص." Meaning: I want to book a bus ticket.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أبي أحجز تذكرة".

exercises.tip: "أحجز" means "book" and needs no "أن" after "أبي".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "فيه _____ للطلاب؟" Meaning: Is there a discount for students?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "فيه خصم للطلاب؟".

exercises.tip: "فيه" means "is there" in Gulf speech.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I want a one-way ticket only."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أبي تذكرة رايح بس".

exercises.tip: "بس" means "only" and "just".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "How long does the trip take?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "كم ياخذ الطريق؟".

exercises.tip: "ياخذ" means "takes" here, as in "how much time it takes".

exercises.prompt: Which one means "Where's the ticket window?"

too_formal.feedback: "أين" is formal. In the Gulf you say "وين".

exercises.tip: "شباك" is a window or booth where you are served.

exercises.prompt: Which one means "I want to confirm the reservation"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أبي أأكد الحجز".

exercises.tip: "أأكد" is "I confirm".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "الباص / يطلع / كم / الساعة"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "الباص الساعة كم يطلع؟".

exercises.tip: Gulf speech often puts the subject first, then the time question.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "بالكرت / أدفع / أقدر"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أقدر أدفع بالكرت؟".

exercises.tip: Two verbs in a row: "can I" then "pay".

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.arabic: هلا، وين كاونتر التسجيل لو سمحت؟
dialogue.transliteration: hala, ween kaawntar it-tasjeel low samaHt?
dialogue.english: Hello, where's the check-in counter please?

dialogue.speaker: Guard
dialogue.english: Over there, after the second gate.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.english: Your passport please.

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: I have my passport and my ticket, here you go.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.english: How many bags do you have?

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Two bags, is this bag overweight?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.english: No, the weight is fine.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.arabic: البوابة اثنعش، والطيارة تطلع الساعة سبعة
dialogue.transliteration: l-bawwaaba ithn3ash, w iT-Tayyaara tiTla3 s-saa3a sab3a
dialogue.english: Gate twelve, and the plane leaves at seven.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.arabic: جوازچ لو سمحت. جاية سياحة لو شغل؟
dialogue.transliteration: jawaazich low samaHt. jaaya siyaa7a low shughul?
dialogue.english: Your passport please. Are you coming for tourism or work?

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Tourism, God willing.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.english: How long will you stay here?

dialogue.speaker: Layla
dialogue.english: Two weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.english: You are most welcome.

pair.english: How many bags am I allowed to take?
Do you have anything to declare?
Are you coming for tourism or work?
How long will you stay here?

lessons.culture: At UAE and Kuwait airports officers greet visitors with "حياك الله", and staff often speak Arabic, English and other languages in the same shift. Say "إن شاء الله" when you talk about your plans, for example how long you will stay, as locals do.

exercises.prompt: The officer says: "جوازك لو سمحت." Say you have your passport and your ticket.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "معاي الجواز والتذكرة".

exercises.tip: "معاي" means "I have with me".

exercises.prompt: The officer asks: "جاي سياحة لو شغل؟" Say tourism.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "سياحة".

exercises.tip: "لو" here means "or", not "if".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "وين _____ الطيارة؟" Meaning: Where's the boarding gate?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "وين بوابة الطيارة؟".

exercises.tip: Gulf speech says "طيارة" for plane.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "كم _____ أقدر آخذ؟" Meaning: How many bags am I allowed to take?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "كم شنطة أقدر آخذ؟".

exercises.tip: "شنطة" is the everyday word for bag or suitcase.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where's the check-in counter?"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "وين كاونتر التسجيل؟".

exercises.tip: "كاونتر" is the word used at the airport.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "How long will you stay here?" (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "كم بتقعد هني؟".

exercises.tip: "بـ" before the verb makes the future, and "هني" is "here".

exercises.prompt: Which one means "No, I don't have anything"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "لا، ما عندي شي".

exercises.tip: "ما عندي" is the everyday way to say "I don't have".

exercises.prompt: Which word means "plane" in everyday Gulf speech?

too_formal.feedback: "الطائرة" is the formal word. Gulf speech says "الطيارة".

exercises.tip: "الطيارة" is used for planes, and "الرحلة" for the flight.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "والتذكرة / معاي / الجواز"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "معاي الجواز والتذكرة".

exercises.tip: "معاي" starts the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "تطلع / الساعة / كم / الطيارة"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "الساعة كم تطلع الطيارة؟".

exercises.tip: "تطلع" means "leaves" for a plane as for a bus.

phrases.arabic: الله يعَوّض، إِن شاء الله يِصير خَير
phrases.transliteration: allah y3awwiD, in shaa allah yiSeer khayr

dialogue.speaker: Fahad
dialogue.english: Excuse me, I lost my bag.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.arabic: لا تخاف، من وين كنت مسافر؟
dialogue.transliteration: laa tkhaaf, min ween kint musaafir?
dialogue.english: Don't worry, where were you travelling from?

dialogue.speaker: Fahad
dialogue.arabic: من الكويت، والطيارة كانت متأخرة مرة
dialogue.transliteration: min l-kuwayt, w iT-Tayyaara kaanat mit2akhkhira marra
dialogue.english: From Kuwait, and the plane was very delayed.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.english: What does the bag look like?

dialogue.speaker: Fahad
dialogue.transliteration: sooda, w kabeera, w inkasrat il-3ajala
dialogue.english: Black and big, and the wheel got broken.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.arabic: زين، بنسجل بلاغ، جوازك لو سمحت
dialogue.transliteration: zeen, bnsajjil balaagh, jawaazak low samaHt
dialogue.english: Good, we'll file a report, your passport please.

dialogue.speaker: Fahad
dialogue.arabic: ما لقيت جوازي، لحظة، إي هذا هو
dialogue.transliteration: ma lageet jawaazi, la7Za, ee hadha huwa
dialogue.english: I couldn't find my passport, wait, yes here it is.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.english: Thank God. Is there another problem?

dialogue.speaker: Fahad
dialogue.english: Yes, I need to change the flight to tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.arabic: أكيد، تقدر تروح مكتب الشكاوي وهم يساعدونك
dialogue.transliteration: akeed, tagdar troo7 maktab ish-shakaawi w hum ysaa3doonak
dialogue.english: Of course, you can go to the complaints office and they will help you.

dialogue.speaker: Fahad
dialogue.english: Nobody answered me there earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.english: I'll call them now. Come with me.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.arabic: إن شاء الله، لا تشيل هم
dialogue.transliteration: in shaa allah, laa tsheel hamm
dialogue.english: God willing, don't worry.

response.english: Don't worry, what does it look like?

pair.english: I missed the bus, what do I do?

response.english: There's another bus in an hour.

pair.english: I missed the flight, what do I do?

response.english: Go to the airline office and change it.
On the first floor, next to the reception.

lessons.culture: When something goes wrong while travelling, Gulf people stay calm and say "الله يعوّض" or "إن شاء الله يصير خير" instead of complaining. Staff in the UAE and Kuwait usually respond to a polite "لو سمحت" and a smile faster than to an angry voice.

exercises.prompt: You reach the counter and lost your bag. Tell the agent.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "ضيّعت شنطتي".

exercises.tip: "ضيّعت" means "I lost".

exercises.prompt: A friend says: "الرحلة تأخرت وانكسرت شنطتك!" Say: May God make up for it, God willing it'll work out.
exercises.answer: الله يعَوّض، إِن شاء الله يِصير خَير
accepted: الله يعَوّض، إِن شاء الله يِصير خَير
allah y3awwiD, in shaa allah yiSeer khayr
الله يعوض إن شاء الله يصير خير

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "الله يعوّض".

exercises.tip: "الله يعوّض" is a calm, everyday way to accept a loss.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ الباص." Meaning: I missed the bus.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "فاتني الباص".

exercises.tip: "فاتني" means "it passed me" and is used for anything you miss.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "ما _____ جوازي." Meaning: I couldn't find my passport.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "ما لقيت جوازي".

exercises.tip: "ما" plus the past verb makes a negative.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "The bag got broken."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "الشنطة انكسرت".

exercises.tip: The subject comes first, and "انكسرت" says it happened by itself.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I missed the flight, what do I do?"

too_formal.feedback: Formal. Gulf speech says "شو أسوي؟" in the UAE and "شنو أسوي؟" in Kuwait.

exercises.tip: "فاتتني" has "ت" because "الرحلة" is feminine, and "ني" means "me".

exercises.prompt: Which one means "Nobody answered me"?

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "محد رد علي".

exercises.tip: "محد" is the short Gulf form of "ما أحد".

exercises.prompt: Which one means "Where's the complaints office?"

too_formal.feedback: "أين" is formal. In the Gulf you say "وين".

exercises.tip: "مكتب" is an office and "شكاوي" are complaints.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "أغيّر / أبي / الرحلة"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "أبي أغيّر الرحلة".

exercises.tip: "أبي" plus a verb is the everyday way to say "I want to do it".

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "مشكلة / فيه / الحجز / في"

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but formal Arabic. Everyday Gulf speech says "فيه مشكلة في الحجز".

exercises.tip: "فيه" starts the sentence and means "there is".

challenge.title: Book a Trip and Handle a Problem
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Gulf Arabic conversation of at least 10 lines. Book a hotel room or a ticket, ask about the price or the time, then something goes wrong while travelling (a delay, a lost bag, or a missed trip). Say what happened and ask for help or a solution.
required_elements: A request for a room or a ticket in a full sentence, such as أبي غرفة لشخصين or أبي أحجز تذكرة
A question about the price or the time, such as بكم؟ or الساعة كم؟
A problem while travelling, such as ضيّعت شنطتي, فاتني الباص or الطيارة متأخرة
A request for help or a solution, and a closing phrase such as الله يعوّض or إن شاء الله يصير خير

dialogue.speaker: Saeed

dialogue.speaker: Clerk

dialogue.english: Twenty-five dirhams, and the bus leaves at nine.

dialogue.speaker: Saeed

dialogue.speaker: Clerk

dialogue.transliteration: laa tkhaaf, fiih baaS thaani ba3d saa3atayn
dialogue.english: Don't worry, there's another bus in two hours.

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.arabic: فيه كرسي فاضي في الباص الثاني؟
dialogue.transliteration: fiih kursi faadi fi l-baaS th-thaani?
dialogue.english: Is there a free seat on the second bus?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.english: Yes, I'll change the ticket for you.

dialogue.speaker: Saeed
dialogue.arabic: الله يعَوّض، إِن شاء الله يِصير خَير
